section.title: The Day of Vengeance
section.sectionRationale: This short, startling oracle answers the question Isaiah 61 left open. A figure approaches from Edom, garments stained crimson like a winepress treader, and identifies Himself as mighty to save. He has trodden the nations alone in judgment because no one else would help. It is the day of vengeance that chapter 61 named but did not yet enact, now pictured in full, sobering color.
section.thesis: The same LORD who saves also judges alone, treading down the nations in righteous wrath when He finds no one to help Him, and this solitary, blood-stained victory is the same divine warrior John later sees returning as Christ, robed and treading the winepress of God's fury.
section.frameNote: Two movements: who is this coming from Edom, crimson-stained, mighty to save; and I trod the winepress alone, for the day of vengeance was in My heart.

units.label: Who is this coming from Edom?

verses.text: Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments? Who is this robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength? “It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save.”
Why are Your clothes red, and Your garments like one who treads the {{gat|winepress}}?

units.label: I have trodden the winepress alone
units.note: the day of vengeance, the year of redemption

verses.text: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with Me. I trampled them in My anger and trod them down in My fury; their blood spattered My garments, and all My clothes were stained.
For the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come.
I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one assisted. So My own arm brought Me salvation, and My own wrath upheld Me.
I trampled the nations in My anger; in My wrath I made them drunk and poured out their blood on the ground.”

gat.gloss: Winepress, the vat where grapes were trodden underfoot to release their juice, the stained garments of the treader a natural, vivid picture. Here the image is turned to judgment, treading down the nations as grapes are trodden, an image John draws on directly for Christ's return in Revelation 19:15, He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty.

basic.context: A lone figure approaches from Edom, His garments stained crimson like a winepress treader. Asked why, He answers that He has trodden down the nations alone in judgment, since no one else would help, and that this was the day of vengeance He had determined and the year of His people's redemption.
basic.hermeneutics: This is deliberately jarring after the gentle mercy of chapters 60 to 62; it insists that the same God who saves also judges, and that His judgment, like His salvation, required Him to act utterly alone. The chapter must be read alongside chapter 61's unfinished sentence, the day of vengeance He named but paused before enacting there is fully pictured here.
basic.originalLanguages: The image is drawn from the gat, winepress, where grapes are trodden until their juice, like blood, stains the treader's garments. The same verb for treading down nations recurs in Revelation, where Christ treads the great winepress of the wrath of God.
basic.typology: This solitary, blood-stained warrior returning from judgment on the nations is the same figure John sees in Revelation 19, a rider called Faithful and True, whose robe is dipped in blood, treading the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty.
basic.christ: Revelation 19:11-16 pictures the returning Christ in language drawn directly from this passage, a warrior on a white horse, robe dipped in blood, treading the winepress of God's wrath, called Faithful and True, King of kings and Lord of lords. Isaiah 63 is the Old Testament's clearest picture of Christ's second coming as righteous Judge, distinct from His first coming as the suffering Servant of chapter 53.
basic.god: God's justice is not a passive withholding, it is an active, righteous response to persistent evil, and He does not delegate it, He acts alone, unaided, precisely because no human agent is righteous enough to execute it rightly. His wrath and His redemption are named together, the day of vengeance and the year of redemption are one and the same act.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 19:11-16 pictures Christ's return using the exact imagery of this passage, robe dipped in blood, treading the winepress. Revelation 14:19-20 describes the great winepress of God's wrath. Isaiah 34:5-8 similarly pictures judgment on Edom as a day of vengeance.
basic.oneStory: The same Servant who was crushed silently in chapter 53 returns here as a warrior who crushes His enemies, and the Bible's whole story holds both truths without contradiction: Christ came once to bear judgment for sinners who trust Him, and He will come again to execute judgment on those who never turned from rebellion.

context.literary:
The six verses are built as a catechism, two questions and two answers, and the lengths are lopsided on purpose. The watcher's first question, verse 1, gets a one line reply that gives a function instead of a name: the figure is the one 'proclaiming vindication, mighty to save.' The second question, verse 2, asks about the colour of the clothes, and that small, almost domestic question releases the long answer of verses 3 to 6. The reader is made to see the stain before being told what caused it.

The answer is wrapped in a double 'alone.' Verse 3 opens with 'no one from the nations was with Me,' and verse 5 returns to the thought with 'there was no one to help' and 'no one assisted.' Between them the first person pronoun is hammered: My anger, My fury, My garments, My heart, My arm, My wrath. Nothing in the scene is shared, delegated or witnessed by anyone else, and the grammar of the passage enacts the solitude it describes.

The passage also plays on sound. In verse 1 the place is Edom, and in verse 2 the clothes are red, and the two words are near twins in Hebrew, as they were when Esau was nicknamed for the red stew, Genesis 25:30. The listener hears the colour before the speaker names the cause.

Its position in the book matters. Isaiah 59:15 to 20 draws almost the same portrait, a LORD who looks for someone to intercede, finds no one, and acts with His own arm, wearing garments of vengeance. Chapters 60 to 62 then open out into glory, a herald and a renamed Zion, and 63:1 to 6 brings the warrior back as the unavoidable other half of that rescue. The salvation of 62:11, 'See, your Savior comes,' arrives here, and it arrives bloodstained. The scene also serves as the hinge into the lament that follows, which begins at 63:7 with a people who have just seen what it costs God to save them.
context.historical:
Edom was the nation descended from Esau, Genesis 36:1, Israel's kinsman and, in Moses' words, 'your brother,' Numbers 20:14. When Israel asked for passage on the King's Highway the Edomites answered with a threat of the sword, Numbers 20:18 to 21, and the grievance never healed. When Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, Edom stood by and then joined the plunder. Obadiah 10 to 14 lists the offences one after another, from standing aloof to cutting off fugitives at the crossroads. Psalm 137:7 remembers the Edomites shouting 'Tear it down to its foundations!', and Ezekiel 35:5 names an 'ancient hatred.'

That is why Edom could serve as the stand in for every hostile nation. Isaiah 34:5 to 8 had already named Bozrah, Edom's chief city, as the place of 'a great slaughter' in 'a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.' The first hearers did not need geography lessons. They knew who had gloated, and they were ready to hear that the account would be settled.

The image of the winepress belonged to harvest season, when grapes were trodden by foot in a stone cut trough so that the juice ran down into a lower vat. Treaders worked in a rhythm of shouting, Jeremiah 25:30, and the work left their clothes soaked and spattered. The prophets already used the picture for judgment, Joel 3:13, and Lamentations 1:15 had turned it against Judah: 'Like grapes in a winepress, the Lord has trampled the Virgin Daughter of Judah.' Isaiah 63 reverses the direction of the treading.

The date of this section of the book is debated. Some place chapters 56 to 66 among the community returning after 538 BC, others hear Isaiah of Jerusalem speaking ahead to that community. Either way the listeners lived with a shattered city and a rival neighbour, and the prophet's answer was that vengeance belongs to the LORD, not to them.
context.canonical:
The passage sits at the end of a chain of earlier texts. Deuteronomy 32:35 and 43 put vengeance in God's hands and tie it to His mercy, 'He will avenge the blood of His children,' and Exodus 15:3 had called Him 'a warrior.' Isaiah 59:16 to 20 gave the warrior a face, and Isaiah 34 gave him a battlefield. Genesis 49:11 pictures Judah's king washing 'his robes in the blood of grapes,' a blessing image of abundance that Isaiah 63 darkens into a battle image.

Isaiah 61:1 to 3 is the nearest neighbour. The anointed herald proclaims 'the year of the LORD's favor and the day of our God's vengeance,' and the second half of that sentence waits for chapter 63. When Jesus reads this passage in Nazareth he stops in the middle of the sentence and does not read the vengeance clause, Luke 4:18 to 21. The church has lived in the gap between the two halves ever since. Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 to say that 'now is the day of salvation,' 2 Corinthians 6:2, and he describes the Lord Jesus 'revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire, inflicting vengeance,' 2 Thessalonians 1:7 and 8.

The book of Revelation is built on this passage. The rider with a robe dipped in blood who 'treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty,' Revelation 19:13 and 15, joins Isaiah 63 to the vintage of Revelation 14:17 to 20. Revelation 19:2 completes the Deuteronomy line: 'He has avenged the blood of His servants.' Paul's counsel to the church fits the same canon, 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet wanted a weary community to see that the promise of 61:2 had a second half and that the second half would be kept. Exiles and returnees had watched Edom and others cheer at Jerusalem's fall, and they were tempted either to despair that wrongs go unanswered or to take matters into their own hands. The passage answers both temptations with one picture. The wrongs are noted, God has the day fixed in His own heart, and the one who settles it needs no assistance and will accept none.

He also meant them to learn something about the shape of rescue. Salvation in this book has never been cheap talk. The figure who is 'mighty to save' is the same figure whose clothes are red, so the hearers are not allowed to love the salvation and ignore the judgment that accompanies it. The nations who opposed Zion are not only a political problem for Israel; they stand against the LORD Himself, and He deals with them personally.

The lament that follows suggests a third purpose. A people who have seen the Warrior's solitary work are in a position to pray honestly, because they know that if anything is going to change it will be because God Himself acts. They cannot send for allies, and neither can He.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what God does; it does not tell anyone to do it. The treading is done 'alone,' and the whole point of that word is to keep the sword out of other hands. Paul draws the practical conclusion in Romans 12:19 to 21, where believers are told not to avenge themselves because vengeance is the Lord's, and are pointed instead to feeding an enemy and overcoming evil with good. The same Jesus who will judge, Acts 17:31, told His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, Matthew 5:44.

The passage also does not hand the reader a map. Edom was a real nation with a real history, and it gives the prophet his stage, but nothing in the text invites a reader to look for the modern equivalent of Edom and to treat it with hostility. The New Testament uses the passage to speak of Christ's return and of the final reckoning, never to license violence between peoples. What carries over directly is confidence and restraint: confidence that wrongs will be answered, and restraint from answering them ourselves. It also carries over as a sober reminder that the mercy being offered now, 2 Corinthians 6:2, is offered inside a limited time.

debates.question: Whose blood is on the Warrior's garments?

views.label: The blood of the enemies
views.case: Verse 3 says 'their blood spattered My garments,' and verse 6 speaks of pouring out 'their blood on the ground.' The picture is a treader whose clothes are stained with the juice of what he has trampled, and the parallel passage in Isaiah 34:6 and 7 also has the LORD's sword drenched with the blood of Edom. The stain is evidence of judgment already carried out.

views.label: The Warrior's own blood, the passion of Christ
views.case: Many church fathers read the red garments as the sign of the Lord's passion. They noticed that in Revelation 19:13 the robe is already 'dipped in blood' before the nations are struck down, which may point to the sacrifice that came first, as in Revelation 5:6 and 7:14. On this reading Isaiah's picture folds the cross into the return.

views.label: Both, held together
views.case: A number of interpreters say the text means what it says, the enemies' blood, while the New Testament's use of it shows that the One who judges is the One who bled, Hebrews 9:12. The two blood stains are not rivals, because the Judge is qualified to condemn partly because He has already borne the sentence for those who come to Him.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew of verses 3 and 6 speaks plainly of the nations, so a reader should start there. The second view enters through the New Testament, not through Isaiah's own words, and it is best held as a layered reading rather than as a replacement of the plain sense.

debates.question: What event does the passage describe?

views.label: A historical judgment on Edom and the nations of the prophet's day
views.case: Edom is named, and Isaiah 34 and Obadiah announce its judgment in similar words. Ancient prophecy often speaks of an immediate judgment in language large enough to carry a final one. The fall of Edom's power in the following centuries, Malachi 1:3 and 4, fits as a first stage.

views.label: The final return of Christ in judgment
views.case: Revelation 19:11 to 16 and 14:19 to 20 take the image up directly and set it at the end of the age, with the nations gathered against God's people. The universal language of 'the nations' and the 'year of My redemption' suggests a day that reaches beyond one small kingdom.

views.label: The cross as the decisive victory
views.case: Some early readers took the lone figure as the Lord at His passion, bearing the blood of the winepress in His own body, and heard 'I looked, but there was no one to help' in Gethsemane and at the arrest, Matthew 26:40 and 56. On this view the judgment on the powers happens in the cross, Colossians 2:15.

debates.bearing: These readings need not exclude one another. A prophet describing a local judgment, a final one and the hinge event between them in one picture would be doing what Isaiah does elsewhere, as with 61:1 to 2 and Luke 4. The safest course is to treat Edom as the first object of the vision and Revelation as its clearest New Testament fulfilment, while letting the cross shape how we understand the Judge.

study.originalLanguages:
The first thing to notice is the sound play between 'Edom' in verse 1 and 'red' in verse 2. Both come from the same root as the colour adom, and the connection goes back to Esau, who was called Edom because of the red stew, Genesis 25:30. The prophet sets a name and a stain next to each other so that the listener understands the colour as a verdict on the nation.

The Warrior describes Himself as 'mighty to save.' The verb for save, hoshia, has the same root as Hosanna, which means 'save, please,' Psalm 118:25, and as the name Joshua, whose later form is Jesus. The title is one of the book's names for God as rescuer, but in this verse it comes out of a mouth stained with the blood of the nations. The word translated 'vindication,' tsedaqah, is the common word for righteousness, and the BSB footnote offers the alternative 'speaking in righteousness.' Either way the Warrior's word and His deed are both right, which is why Revelation 19:11 says 'with righteousness He judges and wages war.'

Verse 2 uses the common word for treading grapes, darak, as in Isaiah 16:10, where no one 'tramples the grapes' in the winepresses. Verse 3 then uses a second word for the winepress, purah, the same word that appears for the vat in Haggai 2:16. The prophet is not repeating himself. He is turning a farm scene around until the reader cannot unsee it. The word translated 'blood' in verses 3 and 6 is one that lexicons commonly gloss as juice or lifeblood, which keeps the grape picture alive inside the battle picture.

The phrase 'day of vengeance' is yom naqam, the same wording as 34:8 and 61:2. The root naqam is not private spite. It is the act of the one with the right to act, repaying wrong and restoring order, and Deuteronomy 32:35 and 43 tie it to God's care for 'the blood of His children.' In verse 4 it is paired with redemption, a pairing the Old Testament law already knew, because the family redeemer, the go'el, was also the 'avenger of blood,' Numbers 35:19. In one office the same figure rescues the kin and answers for the killing.

The verbs in verse 5 repeat the language of Isaiah 59:16. 'I looked' and 'I was appalled' correspond to 'He saw' and 'He was amazed' there, and both appear to come from the same root, shamem, which carries the sense of being stunned or horrified. The BSB reads 'amazed' in chapter 59 and 'appalled' in chapter 63, and both fit: it is the astonishment of someone who expected a response and met silence. The phrase 'My arm brought Me salvation' draws on the book's recurring image of the LORD's arm, 51:9, 52:10 and 53:1, so the Warrior of this passage is the same arm that the Servant Song says would be revealed.

typology.type: The winepress of wrath, Isaiah 63:2 and 3
typology.fulfillment: The grape harvest was Israel's picture of both joy and judgment, and the prophets used it for the second. Joel 3:13 calls the nations to the valley where the winepress is full, and Lamentations 1:15 had cast Judah as the grapes. In Revelation the picture is completed twice: the angel's sickle gathers the earth's vintage into 'the great winepress of God's wrath,' Revelation 14:19, and Christ Himself 'treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty,' Revelation 19:15. The escalation is from a harvest scene to the end of history. The type falls short only in being an image, since it cannot show the moral weight of the verdict, which Revelation 19:2 states plainly: 'His judgments are true and just.'

typology.type: The arm of the LORD that acts alone, Isaiah 63:5
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah speaks of the LORD's arm three times before this chapter, Isaiah 51:9, 52:10 and 53:1, and each time the arm is a person's work in disguise. Here the arm 'brought Me salvation,' because no helper was found. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who acts for His people with no human partner. The disciples all fled, Matthew 26:56, and He said they would 'leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me,' John 16:32. The escalation is that His isolation was real and yet He was never abandoned by the Father in His purpose. The type falls short because the Warrior's solitude here is one of strength, whereas the cross also involved the loneliness of bearing sin.

typology.type: Edom as the brother turned enemy, Isaiah 63:1
typology.fulfillment: Edom is a kinsman nation that hardened into permanent opposition, from Numbers 20:18 to Obadiah 10 to 14. The New Testament does not name Edom as the enemy of Christ's return, so the link is a pattern and not a prediction, but it is a clear one. Revelation's kings and armies gathered against the rider, Revelation 19:19, are the same type of opposition widened to the whole earth. The escalation is from a nation that refused passage to a world order that refuses the King. The type falls short because Edom was a political entity with borders, whereas the opposition at the end belongs to every people, and some from every nation will be on the other side, Revelation 7:9.

Judah's blessing in Genesis 49:11 pictured a king who washes his robe in the blood of grapes, and Revelation 5:5 calls Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah. The red garment of Isaiah 63 becomes the robe 'dipped in blood' of Revelation 19:13. The robe also stands in contrast with other robes in Revelation: the saints 'have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb,' Revelation 7:14. The same blood that marks the Judge cleanses those who come to Him. The type falls short in that the Warrior's garment shows His work against enemies, while the believer's white robe shows a work done for them.

study.christ:
Revelation 19 borrows this passage so openly that the question for a reader is not whether Christ is meant but what the borrowing teaches. Three things stand out when the two texts are laid side by side.

First, the Warrior of Isaiah comes as the answer to a question that chapter 62 raised. Isaiah 62:11 says, 'See, your Savior comes! Look, His reward is with Him,' and Isaiah 59:20 had promised 'the Redeemer will come to Zion.' Paul quotes that last promise in Romans 11:26, applying it to the coming Deliverer. The figure of 63:1 is therefore not a second, rival person. He is the Savior of 62:11, seen from the side of the nations He has to deal with.

Second, the figure is called 'The Word of God' in Revelation 19:13, and in Isaiah 63:1 the first thing He does is speak: 'proclaiming vindication.' In Revelation the weapon in His hands is a sword that proceeds from His mouth, Revelation 19:15, so the battle is fought and won by His word. The Gospel of John says that the Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22, and Paul preached at Athens that God will judge the world 'by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31. The Judge has been named, and He is the Man who was raised from the dead.

Third, the passage insists on the Warrior's solitude, and the Gospels show Jesus entering exactly that solitude. In Gethsemane He asked, 'Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?' Matthew 26:40, and then 'all the disciples deserted Him and fled,' Matthew 26:56. Isaiah 53:10 says it was 'the LORD's will to crush Him,' and Isaiah 63:5 says 'My own wrath upheld Me.' The two pictures meet at the point where the Son takes the wrath that would fall on others, Romans 3:25, and at the end of history takes the office of judge over those who refused it. It is not that Isaiah 63 is a picture of the cross; it is that the Christ who finally treads the winepress has already gone through the cross, so His judgment is never arbitrary.

The 'day of vengeance' also has a pastoral edge. Jesus stopped reading before that clause in Nazareth, Luke 4:19, and Paul hears the offer of favor as still open, 2 Corinthians 6:2. The long delay is not the absence of the second half of the verse but the patience of the One who is 'mighty to save,' Hebrews 7:25. The same Savior who can 'save completely those who draw near to God through Him' is the One whose robe is red for those who will not.

A caution keeps this honest. The prophet speaks in vivid pictures, and not every detail needs a separate fulfilment. The reader should not hunt for an exact referent for Bozrah or the winepress trough, but should follow the New Testament's own handling of the passage: a returning King, a righteous judgment, and a salvation that was paid for before it was announced.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the one who feels the weight of injustice and does something about it. The text says the day of vengeance was 'in My heart,' and the word picture is of a resolve held for a long time before it is carried out. That moves vengeance out of the category of sudden temper. It is a settled commitment of the one who made the world to see it righted, and the prophet places it side by side with 'the year of My redemption.' The God who saves and the God who judges are one God, acting from a single purpose.

The passage also shows God's self-sufficiency in a startling way. He needs no ally, and 'My own wrath upheld Me.' Yet He looked for a helper and 'was appalled that no one assisted.' Both statements stand. The God who does not need anyone still seeks a human intercessor, as Ezekiel 22:30 says, 'I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me,' and finds none. This is not weakness. It is the shape of a relationship in which God wants partners and does not get them, which makes the astonishment real. It points straight forward to the one intercessor who does stand in the gap, Hebrews 7:25.

The passage also holds together attributes that people prefer to separate. God is faithful to His own people and severe toward their oppressors. He is patient and yet there is a day. He is kind and yet He treads. Paul asks the church to look at both, 'the kindness and sternness of God,' Romans 11:22. A theology that keeps only the kindness cannot make sense of Revelation 6:10, where the martyrs cry, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?' A theology that keeps only the severity cannot hear 'mighty to save.'

The passage reveals God's relationship to history. Nations are not outside His account. Edom's gloating at a neighbour's fall is noticed, remembered and answered, Obadiah 12. No tyrant's violence is finally unobserved. The comfort of that is not delight in suffering but trust that a Judge sees.

For worship, the passage teaches fear and relief together. Fear, because a God who settles accounts in person is not to be taken lightly. Relief, because we are not asked to settle our own accounts and are free from the weight of revenge. Praise in the end looks like the 'Hallelujah' of Revelation 19:1 and 2, a cry that salvation and glory belong to God because 'His judgments are true and just.' Before that day, the right response is to leave room for God's wrath, to forgive as we have been forgiven, and to bring the nations the message of the One who is willing to save.

crossReferences.note: The nearest parallel in the book. The LORD looks, finds no one to intercede, and His own arm brings salvation, wearing garments of vengeance and a breastplate of righteousness. Chapter 63 acts out the plan announced there, and verse 20 adds the promise that the Redeemer comes to Zion for those who turn from transgression.

The earlier oracle against Edom. The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood, there is a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a day of vengeance becomes a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. It explains why Edom and Bozrah are named in 63:1, and it shows the passage as part of a long prophetic thread, not a stray image.

The anointed herald proclaims the year of favor and the day of our God's vengeance in one breath. Chapter 63 is the second half of that sentence, so reading the two together stops a reader from treating the gentle promises of chapters 60 to 62 as the whole message.

Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and stops after the year of the Lord's favor, leaving the vengeance clause unread. That choice marks the first coming as the time of favor and leaves the rest for another day, which is the day Isaiah 63 describes.

The rider called Faithful and True wears a robe dipped in blood, strikes the nations with a sword from His mouth and treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God. John does not quote Isaiah 63 by name, but nearly every phrase echoes it, and he gives the Warrior His name, the Word of God.

An angel's sickle gathers the vintage of the earth into the great winepress of God's wrath, trodden outside the city. This parallel shows how thoroughly Isaiah's image shaped the Apocalypse and fills out the scene the same way Joel did before.

The nations are summoned to the valley where the LORD sits to judge, with the call to swing the sickle for the harvest and trample the grapes because the winepress is full. Joel is the nearest prophetic source for the harvest image Isaiah turns into a lone treading.

Jerusalem's own lament says the Lord trampled Judah like grapes in a winepress. Isaiah 63 answers it by reversing the direction of the treading, so that the people who were crushed see the nations that crushed them brought to account.

Jacob's blessing on Judah describes a king who washes his robes in the blood of grapes. The picture is one of abundance and rule, and later readers have taken it as a seed of the Warrior King whose robes are stained in Isaiah and Revelation, the Lion of the tribe of Judah of Revelation 5:5.

Moses calls Edom 'your brother' and asks for peaceful passage, and Edom answers with a threat of the sword. The refusal is the root of the later hostility that Obadiah and Isaiah 63 answer, and it shows that the judgment on Edom concerns a long record, not a sudden anger.

The prophet lists Edom's offences on the day Jerusalem fell: standing aloof, gloating, looting and cutting off fugitives. These are the particular wrongs behind the vengeance of Isaiah 63, and they explain why the hearers would have understood Edom as the obvious example.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 to tell believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath. This is the practical use of Isaiah 63 for the church: because the Warrior acts alone, nobody else is to pick up the sword.

God searches for a man to stand in the gap and finds no one. The line matches Isaiah 59:16 and 63:5 and shows that the lack of a helper is a repeated prophetic theme, one that finds its answer in the single intercessor of Hebrews 7:25.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a murder and a cry. 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground,' God says to Cain, Genesis 4:10, and from that moment every wrong in the world has a witness. Isaiah 63 is the scene where that witness is finally answered in full. It also answers an older conflict, the brothers Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah's womb, Genesis 25:23, whose descendants carried the rivalry into the story of Israel and Edom. The passage sits where the two questions the Bible keeps asking meet: will wrong be answered, and who will do the answering?

The Old Testament's answer builds up in steps. The LORD is 'a warrior,' Exodus 15:3, who fights for His people at the sea. The law makes room for a redeemer who is also an avenger, Numbers 35:19. The prophets warn that Edom and the nations will drink the cup, Lamentations 4:21 and 22, and promise a Redeemer who comes to Zion, Isaiah 59:20. Isaiah 63 gives that Redeemer a body and a stained robe.

The New Testament gathers the threads at one person. The first coming is the year of the Lord's favor, Luke 4:19, and the cross is where the wrath of God and the love of God meet, with the Son taking the blow Himself, Isaiah 53:10 and Romans 3:25. The second coming completes the sentence Jesus left unread: the rider of Revelation 19 treads the winepress, and the martyrs who cried 'How long?' hear the shout, 'He has avenged the blood of His servants,' Revelation 19:2.

The passage also leads past itself. After the winepress comes the new creation, where the problem of vengeance is gone because the problem of evil is gone: 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away,' Revelation 21:4. The blood on the Warrior's robe is the last blood in the Bible that is shed in judgment, and it is meant to be the last. Those who have been redeemed, in the same book, are the ones with white robes, Revelation 7:14. A reader who sees only the red has not yet seen how the story ends. The Warrior's solitary victory makes room for a city with no night, whose gates never shut, Revelation 21:25.

quiz.q: Why are the garments of the figure approaching from Edom stained crimson?

options.text: He has trodden down the nations alone in righteous judgment, like treading grapes in a winepress.
options.note: Verses 2-3 explain the winepress image as judgment on the nations.

options.text: He has been wounded and defeated in battle.
options.note: The text describes Him as victorious, mighty to save, not defeated.

options.text: He is wearing ceremonial red robes with no connection to judgment.
options.note: The color is real, but the text explicitly ties it to trodden blood in judgment, not mere ceremonial dress.

options.text: He has been harvesting grapes for a feast, unrelated to judgment.
options.note: The winepress image is explicitly reinterpreted as trampling the nations in wrath.

quiz.q: Why did the Warrior act alone, according to verse 5?

options.text: He looked for someone to help and found no one, so His own arm brought Him salvation.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly states no one was found to help or assist.

options.text: He refused all offers of help out of pride.
options.note: The text says no one was available to help, not that help was refused.

options.text: The nations had already surrendered before He arrived.
options.note: This is the opposite of the scene; the passage describes active trampling and judgment, not prior surrender.

options.text: Angels fought alongside Him the entire time.
options.note: The text explicitly says no one from the nations, or anyone else named, assisted Him.

quiz.q: How does Revelation 19 use the imagery of Isaiah 63:1-6?

options.text: It applies the same imagery, a robe dipped in blood, treading the winepress, to Christ's second coming as righteous Judge.
options.note: Revelation 19:11-16 draws directly on this passage's imagery for the returning Christ.

options.text: It rejects any connection between Christ and images of judgment.
options.note: Revelation 19 explicitly connects Christ's return to this judgment imagery.

options.text: It applies this imagery only to a human political ruler, not Christ.
options.note: The rider imagery could suggest a human king, but Revelation 19 names Him Faithful and True, King of kings and Lord of lords, identifying Him as Christ.

options.text: It uses entirely unrelated imagery about a wedding feast only.
options.note: While Revelation 19 includes wedding imagery elsewhere, the specific winepress and blood-stained robe imagery echoes Isaiah 63 directly.

quiz.q: How should this passage be understood alongside Isaiah 53's Suffering Servant?

options.text: As two roles of the same Christ, who bore judgment silently at His first coming and will execute judgment openly at His return.
options.note: Revelation 19's identification of Christ as the returning Judge holds both roles together consistently.

options.text: As proof that the Suffering Servant and this Warrior can never be the same person.
options.note: Christian reading, following Revelation 19, holds these as two comings of the same Christ.

options.text: As contradictory pictures that cancel each other out.
options.note: The tension is real and worth wrestling with, but Scripture presents both mercy and justice as consistent, complementary aspects of God's character in Christ.

options.text: As entirely unrelated passages with no bearing on each other.
options.note: Both describe the same divine Servant and Judge at different stages of His mission.

questions: This passage insists that God's justice is real and personal, not distant or abstract. Does your view of God include this side of Him, or only His mercy?
The Warrior looked for someone to help and found no one. Where in your life or your world do you feel the weight of standing nearly alone for what is right?

The day of vengeance and the year of redemption are called the same moment in verse 4. How does it change your view of justice to know that, for those in Christ, judgment and redemption meet at the same cross rather than opposing each other?

Revelation 19 shows the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53 is the same Christ who returns as Judge in Isaiah 63. How does living with real expectation of Christ's return, not just as Savior but as Judge, shape the urgency of your life today?

Edom stands here as an example of persistent, unrepentant hostility toward God's people. Is there a persistent, unrepented pattern of opposition to God in your own life you have not yet reckoned with seriously?

translationNotes.note: Bozrah was Edom's capital city; the wordplay between Bozrah and the Hebrew word for grape harvest, batsir, strengthens the winepress imagery that follows.
Year of My redemption pairs judgment and redemption as a single act; the same year that judges the nations is the year Zion's people are finally and fully redeemed.
